newsitem.title: UK: British newspaper admits Diana spy video a fake.
newsitem.headline: British newspaper admits Diana spy video a fake.

text.p: Britain's top-selling Sun newspaper admitted it had been duped by fraudsters and that a video it had alleged showed Princess Diana cavorting with her former lover James Hewitt was a fake.
In a sensational and embarrassing front page apology to the 35-year-old princess, the newspaper said its had fallen victim "to one of the most elaborate hoaxes of the decade".
"We were conned by cunning fraudsters into believing that two people frolicking together on a poor quality film were the Princess of Wales and her former lover James Hewitt," the newspaper said.
"The Sun apologises profusely to both of them for any hurt or offence caused."

It was one of the most spectacular climbdowns for the tabloid since 1987 when pop singer Elton John won a million pounds ($1.5 million) in libel damages over untrue allegations it published about sex session with male prostitutes.
The Sun had alleged on Tuesday that the so-called "spy video" had confirmed Diana's fears that she had been spied on during the demise of her 15-year marriage to Prince Charles.
But the 80-second grainy black and white video that was also shown on British television was really a low-budget film made in south London for a laugh with Diana and Hewitt lookalikes.
Amateur film-maker Nick Hedges told the Sun's chief competitor, The Daily Mirror, that he made it in the hope that it would help him and the two actors win some comedy work.

"Never in a million years would I have thought this would have been taken seriously," he said. "This film was maliciously stolen and used for financial gain to con the nation. It was never meant for public consumption."
Hedges said he planned to sue for breach of copyright, ownership and confidentiality and vowed that he was determined find out the truth.
"This has caused enormous distress to myself, the two lookalikes involved -- but above all to the Princess of Wales," he said.
Sun editor Stuart Higgins accepted full responsibility for the blunder and said he had been offered the video by two men acting as intermediaries during a clandestine meeting last week.

The newspaper said it had made its best endeavours "to corroborate the contents" which showed a woman stripping down to gym shorts and sports bra and then riding on the back of a man and playfully throwing pillows at him.
Through her spokeswoman, Diana said on Tuesday that she did not recognise either herself or Hewitt in the photographs published in the newspaper.
Hewitt had refused to comment or speculate about the video.
Higgins said he believed The Sun and himself were the victims of a sophisticated hoax aimed at embarrassing the newspaper.
The Sun said the plot began seven months ago with a phone call but its attempts to unravel the events since then ended with non-existent addresses and people using false names.
Diana has admitted adultery with former Gulf war commander Hewitt and, in a sensational television interview in November, said she had "adored" him during their five-year affair.
In the past she has claimed that her phone calls were bugged. Transcripts of alleged calls she made to male friends have been printed in British newspapers.
